messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: summing out int parameters
parts:
We decided a while ago to just sum out the int
parameters wherever we can. It'll be faster to execute per
sample and convergence/exploration should be faster,
too.

(Is this what people call Rao-Blackwellization? I've also
seen it called "collapsed" sampling in the LDA setting
when you integrate out continuous params.)

An example is the Hearts model (BUGS Vol2 Example)
that Jiqiang just checked in (I just love the
diagram for GIT checkins on

http://code.google.com/p/stan/source/list

# Hearts

data {
int(0,) N;
int(0,) x[N];
int(0,) y[N];
int(0,) t[N];
}

parameters {
real alpha;
real delta;
int(0,) state[N]; // these are discrete parameters. the support is 0 or 1 actually. ??
}

transformed parameters {
real(0,1) theta;
theta <- inv_logit(delta);
}

model {
real yap[2];
yap[1] <- inv_logit(alpha);
yap[2] <- 0;

alpha ~ normal(0, 100);
delta ~ normal(0, 100);
for (i in 1:N) {
state[i] ~ bernoulli(theta); // either 0 or 1
y[i] ~ binomial(t[i], yap[state[i] + 1]);
}
}

(Note: the int(0,) should be int(0,1) for state[N] because
it's binary; but that's the parameter we're summing out
so we don't need it at all.)

What we need to do is replace the inner loop statements:

state[i] ~ bernoulli(theta); // either 0 or 1
y[i] ~ binomial(t[i], yap[state[i] + 1]);

with the version that sums out state[i]:

lp__ <- lp__
+ log_sum_exp(log(theta) + binomial_log(y[i],t[i],yap[1]),
log(1.0 - theta) + binomial_log(y[i],t[i],yap[2]));


The increment expression is just an arithmetically stable
version of:

log(theta * binomial(y[i],t[i],yap[1])
+ (1-theta) * binomial(y[i],t[i],yap[2]);

I haven't written this section of the manual yet. But
it's also on the to-do list. You can leave this example
to me and I'll make sure it works when I write the manual
section.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: solving all the "JAGS models"
parts:
On 4/12/12 10:28 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I think that solving all the models in the Jags manual is a good start,

There are no models in the JAGS manual per se.
They released a code tarball that has translations
of the "BUGS models" (see previous message) to JAGS,
but there's no documentation, just the code.
> also solving all the models we care about.

Is there a list somewhere? Are there models we care
about that can't be expressed in BUGS/JAGS?
We should be able to handle anything BUGS/JAGS
does and quite a bit more in terms of expressiveness.

> Probably best to solve models one at a time, developing general tools as needed, rather than trying to anticipate
uses ahead of time.

Too late for that given that our initial menu was
already all of the "BUGS models" and "everything we
care about" (e.g., speed dating, folates, etc.).

Also, it's not a very good strategy
for developing a programming language -- you wind up
with a Frankenstein monster like Perl if you don't
plan ahead for how things are going to be extended.

The big issue on the expressiveness front is Bayesian
non-parametric models. We haven't thought much at
all about those either for expression or implementation.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] solving all the "JAGS models"
parts:
On Fri, Apr 13, 2012 at 1:37 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>  also solving all the models we care about.

Is there a list somewhere?  Are there models we care
about that can't be expressed in BUGS/JAGS?
We should be able to handle anything BUGS/JAGS
does and quite a bit more in terms of expressiveness.

As in the README in src/models/bugs_examples says:

Openbugs's official example webpage: 
http://www.openbugs.info/w/Examples

JAGS does not have an official stuff for examples, I suppose. 
But http://sourceforge.net/projects/mcmc-jags/files/Examples/2.x/
has some BUGS vol1 and vol2 examples. 

And JAGS' author has a R package for BUGS examples:
 https://r-forge.r-project.org/projects/bugs-examples/
This package includes more examples than the previous one, but 
it does not explicitly say which examples are not supported in JAGS.
This package is written in a way you could run any example using 
either JAGS or BUGS.  And I guess that is how the speed 
comparison is done (post this link again:
http://martynplummer.wordpress.com/2010/09/20/how-fast-is-jags/).

--
Jiqiang
